title: Boss: three async bugs from code review
summary: A connection disposed too early, a fan-out that hides all but one failure, and a fire-and-forget that loses its errors.

steps.title: The review
body: You are reviewing a pull request in the reporting service. Production logs from the last release:
fail: Reports.Api[0] System.ObjectDisposedException: Cannot access a disposed object. Object name: 'DbConn'.
warn: Reports.Jobs[0] nightly export: 1 of 3 shards failed: shard-b timed out
(support says shard-c was also broken that night; nothing in the logs)
crit: Reports.Api[0] Unhandled exception. System.InvalidOperationException: audit store unavailable
Each line is one classic async mistake. Fix them one by one.

steps.title: 1. Disposed before it finished
prompt: `CountAsync` opens a connection, starts a query and returns the query's task **without awaiting it**. The `using` disposes the
connection as soon as the method returns, while the query is still running.
Fix **`static Task<int> CountAsync(Func<DbConn> open, string table)`** so the connection stays open until the query has finished,
and is still disposed afterwards. It returns the result of `conn.QueryAsync($"select count(*) from {table}")`.
starter: static Task<int> CountAsync(Func<DbConn> open, string table)
solution: static async Task<int> CountAsync(Func<DbConn> open, string table)
template: Dojo.Check("The connection is still open while the query runs", !dojoConn.Disposed, "The connection was disposed before the query finished.");
await Dojo.TryAsync("The query completes", async () => { dojoCount = await dojoTask; });
Dojo.Eq("CountAsync returns the query's result", 42, dojoCount);
Dojo.Check("The connection is disposed afterwards", dojoConn.Disposed, "Keep the using: the connection must still be closed when the query is done.");
Dojo.Eq("The SQL names the table", "select count(*) from orders", dojoConn.Sql);
public Task<int> QueryAsync(string sql) { Sql = sql; return Run(); }
async Task<int> Run() { var n = await _result.Task; if (Disposed) throw new ObjectDisposedException("DbConn"); return n; }
hints: Returning a task from inside a `using` without awaiting it ends the `using` scope immediately.
Make the method `async` and `return await conn.QueryAsync(...)`: the `using` then ends after the query completes.
explain: "Eliding" `async`/`await` (returning the task directly) saves a state machine, and it is fine for a one-line pass-through. It is a
bug as soon as the method has a `using`, a `try`/`catch`/`finally`, or a lock around the call: all of those end at the `return`.

steps.title: 2. Every failure, not just the first
prompt: The nightly export runs one job per shard with `await Task.WhenAll(jobs)`. When two shards fail, the log shows only one:
`await` rethrows only the **first** exception of the combined task.
Write **`static async Task<List<string>> RunAllAsync(IEnumerable<Func<Task>> jobs)`** that starts every job, waits for **all** of
them (even when some fail), and returns the `Message` of **every** failure, in the order the jobs were given. No failures: an empty
solution: // all.Exception holds every failure; the catch only stops the first one from escaping
template: async Task DojoFail(string m) { await Task.Yield(); throw new TimeoutException(m); }
var dojoErrors = await RunAllAsync(new Func<Task>[] { DojoOk, () => DojoFail("shard-b timed out"), () => DojoFail("shard-c timed out") });
Dojo.Eq("Both failures are reported, in order", new List<string> { "shard-b timed out", "shard-c timed out" }, dojoErrors);
var dojoNone = await RunAllAsync(new Func<Task>[] { DojoOk, DojoOk });
Dojo.Eq("No failures gives an empty list", new List<string>(), dojoNone);
hints: Keep the list of tasks. After `await Task.WhenAll(...)` (inside a try/catch), each task knows whether it faulted.
`tasks.Where(t => t.IsFaulted).Select(t => t.Exception!.InnerException!.Message)`; or read `all.Exception.InnerExceptions` from the WhenAll task.
explain: The `Task` returned by `WhenAll` keeps an `AggregateException` with **all** the failures; `await` just rethrows the first. Logging
only the caught exception is how incidents lose half their evidence.

steps.title: 3. Fire-and-forget that does not crash the process
prompt: After each request the API writes an audit record without waiting for it, using `async void Audit(...)`. When the audit store is
down, the exception escapes on the thread pool and **the whole process exits**.
Write **`static Task FireAndForget(Func<Task> work, Action<Exception> onError)`**: it starts `work`, returns a task that **never
faults**, and passes any exception from `work` to `onError` (exactly once). It must not block, and must not wait for `work` before
starter: static async void FireAndForget(Func<Task> work, Action<Exception> onError)
solution: static Task FireAndForget(Func<Task> work, Action<Exception> onError)
template: async Task DojoAudit() { await dojoGate.Task; throw new InvalidOperationException("audit store unavailable"); }
Dojo.Check("FireAndForget returns while the work is still running", !dojoTask.IsCompleted, "It waited for the work to finish.");
try { await dojoTask; } catch { dojoFaulted = true; }
Dojo.Check("The returned task never faults", !dojoFaulted, "The exception escaped: catch it inside and hand it to onError.");
Dojo.Eq("onError got the exception once", new List<string> { "audit store unavailable" }, dojoErrors);
Dojo.Eq("Successful work reports no error", 0, dojoOkErrors);
hints: Return a `Task` from an async method that wraps `await work()` in try/catch.
`static Task FireAndForget(Func<Task> work, Action<Exception> onError) { return Run(); async Task Run() { try { await work(); } catch (Exception e) { onError(e); } } }`
explain: In a real service, prefer not to fire and forget at all: hand the work to a `Channel` read by a `BackgroundService` (module 7), so it
survives a slow store, is drained on shutdown, and has backpressure. When you must fire and forget, at least observe and log the error.
